clue.text: Attribute of C. G. Rossetti's winding road

definitions.text: Attribute of C. G. Rossetti's winding road

parts.words: Attribute of C. G. Rossetti's winding road
parts.note: Christina Georgina Rossetti's poem Up-Hill asks whether the road winds uphill all the way, so the quality of that road is its upward slope

explanation.surface: A literary question about the defining feature of a road in a Victorian poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on Up-Hill by Christina Rossetti, whose road winds uphill all the way; the answer is the formal word for an upward slope.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an upward gradient, which is exactly the property of a road that climbs the whole way.

clue.text: Greatly surprised to see a good man 'unted

parts.note: ST, for saint, is the usual crossword good man
the apostrophe drops the H, so this is hounded or hunted said without its first letter

explanation.surface: Amazed to see a saint hunted down, in a dropped-H accent.
explanation.walkthrough: ''unted' is hunted with its H dropped; take the synonym hounded and drop its H to get OUNDED.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dumbfounded or amazed is being greatly surprised.

clue.text: See a man of honour take in a rogue

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order
to eat is to take in food

explanation.surface: A distinguished man is told to take in a scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: CH, Companion of Honour, is a British order; 'take in' is not 'deceive' here but eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler is a rogue who deceives others.

clue.text: ed ahead of the rest

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'ed ahead of the rest (2,3,3)': the first word is cut off in the feed and smudged on the scan, so the opening wordplay or definition is missing

clue.text: Repaired fence, fit for practical purposes

indicators.note: repaired means put back together, so the letters of the two words are reassembled

explanation.surface: A mended fence is fit for use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repaired' makes the letters of FENCE and FIT into a new arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'in practice' or 'virtually', which is what for practical purposes says.

clue.text: Position of a Bohemian peasant

parts.note: in the carol Good King Wenceslas, the Bohemian king places the poor man with an old word meaning over there

explanation.surface: A question about where a Czech farm labourer stands.
explanation.walkthrough: The carol Good King Wenceslas (he was Duke of Bohemia) asks about the peasant 'over there' using an old word for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for 'over there' gives where the peasant stood in the carol.

clue.text: The bell's tolling for king and mistress

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king
Nell Gwyn was the famous mistress of King Charles II

explanation.surface: The bell tolls for a dead king and his mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Gwyn, the orange-seller and actress, was Charles II's mistress, so 'mistress' gives NELL beside K for king.
explanation.definitionFit: The slow ringing of a bell for a death is its tolling.

clue.text: Win in the ring, brave spirit

parts.note: KO, a knockout, wins a boxing bout
bold means brave

explanation.surface: A boxer wins with a courageous fighting spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like courage, but it is the German household goblin of folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: A goblin of German folklore that haunts mines and houses is a kind of sprite.

clue.text: " With sweet musk-roses, and with" (M. N. Dream)

definitions.text: " With sweet musk-roses, and with" (M. N. Dream)

parts.words: " With sweet musk-roses, and with" (M. N. Dream)
parts.note: Oberon's speech in A Midsummer Night's Dream describes a bank overcanopied with woodbine and musk-roses; the missing last word of the line is a sweet briar

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare left for the solver to complete.
explanation.walkthrough: Complete Oberon's line: the bank is canopied 'With sweet musk-roses, and with' a wild rose also called sweet briar.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the sweet briar, a wild rose, which completes Shakespeare's verse.

clue.text: I sell twisted thread

indicators.note: twisted suggests the letters are wound round into a new order, as fibres are

explanation.surface: A trader who sells spun yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisted' rearranges I SELL; it also fits the twisted cotton of the thread.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine, tightly twisted cotton yarn, once used for stockings, is a type of thread.

clue.text: Operational centre for spare parts?

parts.note: a surgical operating room is where operations happen and spare parts are transplanted in; read again, a playhouse is the place where actors take parts

explanation.surface: A depot where spare parts for machines are handled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare parts' suggests a warehouse, but it plays on transplant surgery in an operating room and on the parts actors play on a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a surgical operating room and a playhouse for drama, covering both readings.

clue.text: Tampers with a note in the aristocracy

indicators.note: in tells us the note sits inside the word for aristocrats

parts.note: nobles are members of the aristocracy
B is a musical note

explanation.surface: Someone meddles with a message passed among the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' reads as a written message, but it is the musical note B, put inside NOBLES.
explanation.definitionFit: To nobble a horse or a juror is to interfere with it illicitly, so the verb is a synonym.

clue.text: Free badge of world organization membership

parts.note: UN is the United Nations, the world organization
a club or school tie is worn as a badge of membership

explanation.surface: A badge that comes free with membership of an international body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badge of ... membership' frames the tie, as in an old school tie; 'world organization' slots in to make a UN tie.
explanation.definitionFit: To loosen a knot or bond is to set something loose, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Lone wolf unimpeded by a weapon

parts.note: free means unimpeded or unrestricted
a lance is a long knight's weapon

explanation.surface: A solitary wolf roams unhindered past a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from the hired knights who sold their lances to any lord.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone working independently for no single employer is a lone operator, the idiom here.

clue.text: Bones and Stanley within range

indicators.note: within shows the short name is placed inside the word for bones

parts.note: dice were once made of bone and are called bones in slang
Stan is the usual short form of Stanley

explanation.surface: A doctor called Bones and a man named Stanley are nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones' looks like a nickname, as for a ship's doctor, but it is old slang for dice, which were once carved from bone; 'within' sets the short name inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Range and this word both mean the length between two points.

clue.text: Sequences of notes heard from The Sunbeams

indicators.note: heard tells us to say the notes phrase aloud and write what it sounds like

parts.note: sol and la are notes of the sol-fa scale, and arrays are ordered sequences

explanation.surface: A band called The Sunbeams plays runs of notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'sol-la arrays' (the sol-fa notes sol and la in ordered rows) and you hear the phrase for beams from the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Beams of light coming from our star are what the phrase names.

clue.text: Benign type

definitions.meaning: a type is a sort or category

explanation.surface: A gentle sort of person.
explanation.definitionFit: Benign means gentle and well-disposed, an adjective sense; type is a sort or class, the noun sense of the same word.

clue.text: Hinder man from cleaning

parts.note: to deter is to hinder or discourage
a gent is a man

explanation.surface: Someone stops a man from doing the housework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaning' is an adjective here: the answer can mean cleansing as well as a soap.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means cleansing, the same as cleaning in 'a cleaning agent'.

clue.text: He scores in the ring, missing the bull's-eye

definitions.text: He scores in the ring, missing the bull's-eye

parts.words: He scores in the ring, missing the bull's-eye
parts.note: a bullfighter scores with the crowd and marks the animal in the bullring, aiming at a bull rather than a dartboard

explanation.surface: A darts player hits the outer ring but misses the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scores', 'ring' and 'bull's-eye' paint darts; the ring is a bullring and the man is a bullfighter, after the bull's hide, not the target's centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullfighter performs in the bullring and wounds the animal, never a target's centre.

clue.text: Savage poet lost his head and ran as a Republican

indicators.note: lost his head says the poet's name drops its first letter

parts.note: Walter Savage Landor was an English poet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wild poet panicked and fled as a political rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage' is not wild: it is the middle name of Walter Savage Landor, who loses L to leave ANDOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Andorra was often called a republic, so a native was a citizen of that small state.

clue.text: Ran away back to old Chinatown

indicators.note: back tells us the word for ran away is read from right to left

parts.note: fled means ran away

explanation.surface: Someone flees back to the Chinese quarter of an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinatown' is split as china plus town: the old spelling of Delft, the Dutch town, also names its glazed earthenware.
explanation.definitionFit: Glazed earthenware made in Delft took the town's name, an old spelling covering both pottery and place.

clue.text: Most like the Clyde lassie

parts.note: Bonnie Parker was Clyde Barrow's partner, and a lass from the River Clyde in Scotland is called bonnie; most like her asks for the superlative

explanation.surface: Praise for the girl who most resembles a Glasgow lass.
explanation.walkthrough: The Clyde is Glasgow's river, and Scots call a pretty girl bonnie; the superlative also fits Bonnie of Bonnie and Clyde.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of the Scots word for pretty means the prettiest of all.

clue.text: Mounts at £25 each

definitions.meaning: in British slang a pony is twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: Horses offered for sale at a fixed price.
explanation.walkthrough: A pony is British betting slang for £25, so the plural is so many lots of that sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounts are small horses to ride; in British slang a pony is twenty-five pounds, so these are sums of that amount each.

clue.text: Begins wild sprees

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters run riot and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A night of excess gets going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges BEGINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bouts of indulgence in drink or food are sprees.

clue.text: Agree damage to. Zion, perhaps, up to a point

parts.note: harm means damage

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of the place name may be reordered

parts.note: E is a point of the compass, east

explanation.surface: A plea to agree that harm to Zion is acceptable, up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' reorders the place name, and 'up to a point' adds a compass point at the end; 'to' and 'up to' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on together in tune or opinion is to concur, the sense of agree here.

clue.text: Families used to be, it's on the cards

definitions.text: Families used to be, it's on the cards

parts.words: Families used to be, it's on the cards
parts.note: a children's card game names families by a cheerful adjective, and families were once said to be cheerful in that way

explanation.surface: A forecast that families will be as they once were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's on the cards' sounds like 'likely', but it is the card game named after cheerful families.
explanation.definitionFit: The card game's title calls families cheerful, which families were once thought to be.

clue.text: Space where the route was rough

indicators.note: was rough suggests the letters of the road word are knocked about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A stretch of land where the road was bumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space' looks like empty ground; it points to the word that comes before space in the phrase for the cosmos beyond Earth's air.
explanation.definitionFit: Outer space is the void beyond the atmosphere, so the adjective stands in for that region.

clue.text: Get in touch

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Get in touch (5)': TINGE is an anagram of GET IN, but no clue word signals the anagram unless 'touch' does two jobs as definition and indicator

clue.text: The actor's field ?

parts.note: an actor's work is performing a part, and a sports pitch is called this kind of field

explanation.surface: A question about an actor's area of expertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Field' suggests a profession; it is the sports pitch, named by the same word that describes an actor at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting a role is this activity, and a games pitch is a field for it.

clue.text: Upset, sounded in the river

indicators.note: in says the word for sounded is placed inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
rang means sounded, as a bell does

explanation.surface: Someone is disturbed by a noise heard on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounded' looks like a homophone signal, but here it is the past tense of a bell ringing, set 'in' the river's name; the Dee flows through Wales, England and Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset an arrangement or a mind is to throw it into disorder, a synonym.

clue.text: They may put the nose soundly out of joint

definitions.text: They may put the nose soundly out of joint

parts.words: They may put the nose soundly out of joint
parts.note: nose said aloud is noes, the votes against; the votes in favour can defeat them and so put their nose out of joint

explanation.surface: Something that might break a nose firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' tells us to hear 'nose' as noes, the votes against; votes in favour outnumber them, putting their nose out of joint (upsetting them).
explanation.definitionFit: Votes in favour are the opposite of noes and can outvote and upset them.

clue.text: Precise number ruined following racehorses

indicators.note: following places the reordered number after the racehorses

parts.note: a string is the set of racehorses kept by one stable

indicators.note: ruined indicates the number's letters are wrecked and reordered

parts.note: ten is a number

explanation.surface: An exact figure was spoiled after looking at the horses.
explanation.walkthrough: A trainer's string is the stable's set of racehorses; 'ruined' reorders the number and 'following' puts it after them.
explanation.definitionFit: Strict and exacting rules are precise and demanding, a synonym here.
